title: From Scheme of Work to Daily Lesson
summary: See how the year map, the scheme of work and the lesson plan fit together, and learn five steps that turn one row of a scheme into a clear lesson with objectives and success criteria.

sections.h: Welcome to Week 4: from planning to teaching
p: In Week 3 you built your year map and a scheme of work for one theme. This week you move into the classroom. You will turn each row of your scheme into a real lesson, and you will learn how to make that lesson work for 50 to 60 minutes.

Good teachers do not make a new plan from nothing every night. They use the scheme of work as a guide and ask: What must my students be able to do by the end of today? What will they do to get there? How will I know?
This week you will learn to:
• Use a four-column scheme of work in daily teaching.
• Build a 50 to 60 minute lesson with a starter, main phases and a plenary.
• Join reading and listening to writing and speaking in one sequence.
• Use past papers and the specimen paper without turning every lesson into a test.

b: Find your Week 3 scheme of work and your year map.
Pick the module you will teach next.
Keep a notebook open for lesson ideas.

sections.h: The three layers of planning, and the golden thread
p: Planning has three layers. Each layer is smaller and more detailed than the one before.
• Long-term plan (the year map): about 36 to 40 weeks, with modules, mock exams and an exam buffer.
• Medium-term plan (the scheme of work): one theme of 4 to 6 weeks, with tasks, resources and assessment.
• Short-term plan (the lesson plan): one lesson, with clear stages and times.

The golden thread joins the layers together. It starts at the syllabus aims, goes to the module target, then to the lesson objective, then to the task, and ends with the check. If one link is missing, the lesson may be fun but will not help the exam.
Example of a golden thread:
• Syllabus skill W2: organise ideas into a coherent text using linking devices.
• Module target: I can link my ideas with also, however and because.
• Lesson objective: by the end of the lesson, students can use three linking words in a short paragraph.
• Task: students fix a paragraph with no linking words, then write their own.
• Check: each student shows one sentence with a linking word on the way out.

b: Can I say which syllabus skill this lesson supports?
Is there a task that gives students practice at this skill?
Is there a moment when I check what they learned?

sections.h: How to read one row of your scheme of work
p: Before you plan a lesson, read the row of the scheme very slowly. Ask four questions.
• What is the timeline? Which weeks or lessons does this row cover?
• What are the objectives? What will students be able to do?
• What are the core tasks and skills? Which parts of reading, writing, listening and speaking are practised?
• How will learning be assessed? What evidence will I collect?
Here is an example row from a scheme (written for this course):
• Timeline and objectives: Weeks 5 to 6. I can write an informal email that explains a problem and what I plan to do.
• Core tasks and skills: read a model email; listen to two people describing a problem; plan three paragraphs; write 120 to 160 words; speak for one minute about a problem.
• Resources and technology: model email, a short audio, a checklist, a timer, phones for voice notes.
• Assessment methods: peer check with the checklist; teacher marks one draft with the Content and Language tables.
This one row can become four or five lessons. Your job is to decide how to share the tasks across the lessons.

b: Lesson 1: read the model email and notice the features.
Lesson 2: listen to problems and practise useful language.
Lesson 3: plan and write a first draft.
Lesson 4: peer check, improve and speak about the problem.
Lesson 5: check with the mark scheme and give feedback.

sections.h: Five steps from scheme of work to lesson plan
p: Use these five steps every time. With practice they take about 20 minutes.
• Step 1: Choose the row and the lesson. Decide where this lesson sits in the sequence.
• Step 2: Write one to three objectives and the success criteria. Say what students will do, in simple words.
• Step 3: Choose the tasks. Think input, then practice, then output. Keep each task short.
• Step 4: Choose the resources. List every paper, audio file, picture and tool, and prepare a backup.
• Step 5: Plan the check. Decide how you will see whether students reached the objective.
Then write the timings. Add them up. If the total is more than the lesson, cut a task. Never cut the plenary.

b: Add every stage. Does it fit 50 to 60 minutes?
Have I left five minutes for things that go wrong?
Which task will I cut if I run late?

sections.h: Writing good lesson objectives and success criteria
p: A lesson objective says what students will be able to do. It uses a verb that you can see or hear: write, say, find, match, choose, explain, compare.
Weak objectives: 'To learn about the passive.' 'To do Exercise 3.' 'To discuss holidays.' These say what the teacher will cover or what the page is, not what students can do.
Strong objectives:
• By the end of the lesson, students can find three details in a text and answer short questions with the exact words they need.
• Students can write an email opening and closing that sound friendly.
• Students can give an opinion with one reason and one example.

Success criteria are small steps that show the objective is reached. Write two or three: 'I used 'because' to give a reason.' 'I answered with a word or short phrase, not a sentence.' 'I included all three bullet points.'

Link objectives to the syllabus skill codes when you can. For example, R3 (identify and select details for a specific purpose), W2 (organise ideas with linking devices), L2 (understand opinions and attitudes), S3 (a range of vocabulary). This helps you see which skills you have practised and which you have missed.

ex.t: Turn a weak objective into a strong one
b: Weak: 'To read the text about cities.'
Strong: 'To find five facts in a text about cities and write them as short notes.'
Weak: 'To practise speaking.'
Strong: 'To give a one-minute answer with a reason and an example.'

sections.h: Planning a week, not a single lesson
p: Students remember more when new language comes back in different lessons. So plan a week as a chain. Use the same language focus in reading, listening, speaking and writing across the week.
Here is a simple weekly plan for a four-lesson week (for a class that meets four times):
• Lesson 1: Input. A text or audio on the theme. New language in context. Short practice.
• Lesson 2: Practice. Controlled and guided tasks with the new language. Pair talk.
• Lesson 3: Production. A longer speaking or writing task. Teacher monitors and collects errors.
• Lesson 4: Review and exam skill. Feedback on errors, redo the task, an exam-style exercise and a short quiz.

Homework should link to the next lesson. For example, ask students to read a short text at home and bring two questions. Or ask them to prepare a one-minute talk. Do not use homework only to finish what you did not do in class.

b: Mon: input.
Tue: practice.
Wed: production.
Thu: review and exam skill.
Each lesson ends with a check.

p: Avoid these traps:
• Too many tasks. Six tasks in 50 minutes means none is done well. Choose three or four.
• No time for the plenary. If it is always cut, you never see what students learned.
• All teacher talk. If you speak for more than a third of the lesson, plan more pair and group work.
• No link to the exam. Fun tasks are good, but each should build a skill from the syllabus.
• Copying a lesson from the internet without changing it. Adapt it for your class level, your time and your resources.
• A plan with no backup. Have a printed copy if the internet fails. Have a short task ready for fast finishers.

b: Is my lesson realistic for my class size and my room?
Have I planned for fast finishers and for students who need help?
Is everything I need ready before the lesson starts?

activity: Choose one row from your Week 3 scheme of work. Write the lesson objective, two success criteria, three tasks and the check for one lesson. Time each stage and add the minutes. Ask a colleague to read it and say what students will do in each minute.

check.q: What is the 'golden thread' in planning?
o: The link from the syllabus aim to the lesson task and the check
A thread that joins the pages of the lesson plan
A list of the best tasks for every lesson
The marks students earn in a week

check.q: Which is the strongest lesson objective?
o: Students can find three details in a text and write them as short notes
To read page 24 of the book
To discuss the text with the class

check.q: If your plan has too much for the time, what should you do?
o: Cut a task but keep the plenary
Give all the extra tasks as homework

title: The Four-Column Scheme of Work in Practice
summary: Use a four-column scheme of work with the columns Timeline and Objectives, Core Tasks and Skills, Resources and Technology, and Assessment Methods, and study a worked two-week example with eight lessons.

p: A scheme of work works best as a simple table with four columns. Each column answers one question.
• Column 1: Timeline and objectives. When will it happen, and what will students be able to do?
• Column 2: Core tasks and skills. What will students do, and which skills does it train?
• Column 3: Resources and technology. What do I need to teach it?
• Column 4: Assessment methods. How will I know students learned it, and what will I do with the information?

In Week 3 you used four columns for a whole module: theme and timeline, language focus, exam skill focus and assessment goal. This week we use a version made for daily teaching. Here is how they match:
• Theme and timeline becomes Column 1 (and you add objectives).
• Language focus and exam skill focus become Column 2 (core tasks and skills).
• New in this version: Column 3, resources and technology.
• Assessment goal becomes Column 4, with more detail about the method.

b: You can see the whole unit on one page.
You can check that every lesson has a task, a resource and a check.
Colleagues can read it and teach from it.

p: Write lesson numbers or dates, not only weeks. For example: Lessons 1 to 4 (Week 5). Then write one clear objective for each lesson or each pair of lessons.
Use 'I can' statements. Link them to syllabus skill codes.
Examples:
• Lesson 1 (R1, R3): I can find specific facts in a short article.
• Lesson 2 (W3): I can use five new adjectives in sentences.
• Lesson 3 (S2): I can speak for one minute on a topic with a reason.
• Lesson 4 (W2, W4): I can write an email that is organised and friendly.
If the objectives do not show a clear growth over the lessons, add steps. Lesson 4 should be harder than lesson 1.

b: Leave a small gap for review in each week.
Write the exam date and the mock date at the top.
Mark bank holidays and school events.

p: Core tasks are the main activities that train the skills. For each lesson, list two or three. Say which skill each one trains. Mark each as receptive (reading, listening) or productive (writing, speaking).
Example for one lesson:
• Task 1 (listening, receptive): listen to two short recordings and choose the best picture. Exercise 1 style.
• Task 2 (speaking, productive): in pairs, say which sport you prefer and why.
• Task 3 (writing, productive): write three sentences with 'because'.

Check across the whole unit: Is there a good balance of receptive and productive work? Do students practise all four skills each week? Is the Cambridge exam task type clear, for example Exercise 3 notes, or Part 2 short talk?
If a task is not obviously linked to a skill, ask why you are doing it.

b: Count receptive tasks and productive tasks across the unit.
If most are receptive, add a speaking or writing task.
If most are productive, add input first.

p: List everything you need for every task. This stops last-minute stress. Think about three kinds of resources.
• Texts and audio: past paper texts, textbook pages, a news article, a short recording.
• Materials you make: worksheets, picture cards, checklists, speaking cards.
• Tools and technology: a projector, a speaker, a phone voice recorder, a timer, a class shared folder.
Plan for places where technology is weak. For every digital resource, write a low-tech backup.
• If there is no projector, write the text on large paper or give each pair a printed copy.
• If there is no speaker for audio, read the script aloud yourself and record it on a phone first.
• If the internet is slow, download files before the lesson.
• If students have no phones, use pair talk and write notes on paper.
Keep a folder, on paper or on a computer, for each module. Put every resource in it with a clear name. The next teacher, or you next year, will thank you.

b: Do I have enough copies for the class?
Have I tested the audio?
Is there a backup if the technology fails?
Where is it saved?

p: Assessment tells you whether the lesson worked. Choose the method for each lesson.
Formative methods (during learning):
• Observation of pair work with a simple tally.
• Exit tickets: one question on a slip of paper.
• Quick quizzes of five questions.
• Peer checks with a checklist.
• Short writing marked with the Content and Language tables.
Summative methods (at the end of a unit):
• A past paper exercise marked with the mark scheme.
• A full mock paper.
• A recorded speaking test marked with the four criteria.
For each method write who marks (teacher, peer or self), what criteria are used, and what happens next (feedback, redo, reteach). Without the last part, assessment is just a score.

b: Quick check for understanding: exit ticket.
Practice of an exam skill: one exercise from a past paper.
Progress over time: a mock test every term.
Skill awareness for students: self-assessment checklist.

sections.h: A worked example: two weeks on 'Where we live'
p: Here is a full example for a class that meets four times a week. It is written for this course. The theme is housing and home life, which is common in the exam. The exam skills are Exercise 3 notes, Exercise 5 email and Paper 3 Part 2 talk.

Week 1, Lesson 1. Objective (R1, R3): I can find facts in a short article about homes. Tasks: skim and scan an article; answer six short questions; pair talk about your home. Resources: article, worksheet. Assessment: check answers together; exit ticket.

Week 1, Lesson 2. Objective (W3): I can use words for rooms, furniture and size. Tasks: word map; describe a picture; write five sentences. Resources: picture cards, vocabulary list. Assessment: peer check of sentences.

Week 1, Lesson 3. Objective (L2): I can understand opinions about living in a small home. Tasks: listen to three short speakers; match each speaker to an opinion; discuss. Resources: audio or script, speaker. Assessment: mini quiz.

Week 1, Lesson 4. Objective (S2): I can compare two options and say which I prefer. Tasks: look at a Part 2 style card (two types of home); one minute to prepare; speak for two minutes in pairs. Resources: card, timer. Assessment: peer feedback with two stars and a wish.
Week 2, Lesson 5. Objective (R1, R3): I can write brief notes under headings. Tasks: read a text about tiny homes; complete notes (Exercise 3 style). Assessment: mark with the key.
Week 2, Lesson 6. Objective (W2): I can link ideas with 'because', 'although' and 'however'. Tasks: link sentences; fix a paragraph. Assessment: exit ticket.

Week 2, Lesson 7. Objective (W1, W4): I can write an informal email that explains a problem with my home. Tasks: read a model; plan; write 120 to 160 words. Assessment: peer check, then teacher marks one draft.
Week 2, Lesson 8. Review. Tasks: improve the email using feedback; speak for one minute about a problem at home; five-question quiz on the unit. Assessment: quiz and reflection.

ex.t: What makes this a good unit
b: Every lesson has an objective, a task, a resource and a check.
The skills rotate: reading, writing, listening, speaking.
Each lesson prepares for the next.
The last lesson allows review and a second try.

activity: Fill in a four-column table for two weeks of your own teaching, with at least eight lessons. For each lesson write the objective, the main tasks and skill, the resources and the assessment method. Underline anything that depends on technology and write a backup.

check.q: Which column lists projectors, audio files and worksheets?
Why write a low-tech backup in Column 3?
o: Technology can fail, and the lesson must still work
To make the plan look longer

check.q: Which pair shows a formative and a summative method?
o: Exit ticket and a full mock paper
A mock paper and an end-of-year exam

title: Lesson Micro-Structure: Starter, Main Phases and Plenary
summary: Turn the syllabus into a 50 to 60 minute lesson with a starter, three main interactive phases and a plenary, using timings, a template and a full sample lesson on an informal email.

sections.h: What a 50 to 60 minute lesson looks like
p: A good lesson has a clear shape. Students know where they are, what they are doing and why. The shape has four parts: a starter, the main interactive phases, a plenary and a short close.
Here is a model for a 55 minute lesson.
• Starter: 5 to 8 minutes. Wake up the class and link to the last lesson.
• Main phase 1, Input: 10 to 12 minutes. Students meet the new language or skill in a text, an audio or a model.
• Main phase 2, Guided practice: 10 to 12 minutes. Students practise with support, often in pairs.
• Main phase 3, Free production: 12 to 15 minutes. Students use the language in a speaking or writing task of their own.
• Plenary: 5 to 8 minutes. Check learning against the objective.
• Close: 1 to 2 minutes. Homework and a clear sentence about the next lesson.

img.alt: A timeline bar showing a 55 minute lesson split into starter, input, guided practice, free production and plenary
img.cap: A 55 minute lesson: starter, three main phases and a plenary. The times can move, but the order helps students.

b: For a 40 minute lesson: shorten each phase, keep the plenary.
For a double lesson of 90 minutes: repeat the main phases twice with a short break.
If the class is slow, cut free production to a shorter task, not the plenary.

p: The starter has four jobs. It gets students into English. It recalls the last lesson. It prepares the mind for today's topic. It shows you who is ready.
A good starter is short, easy to explain, and needs little preparation. It should be active and use English. It should never be the same every day.
Examples (more in Unit 25):
• Show a picture and ask students to write five words about it in one minute.
• Put three true or false statements about last lesson on the board.
• Write a jumbled sentence for students to put in order.
Do not start with a long talk from the teacher. Students should be doing something in the first minute.

b: Is it short?
Does it use English?
Does it link to the objective?
Can I run it with no extra material?

p: In the input phase students meet the new skill, text or language. Your aim is understanding, not perfection.
Examples of input:
• A reading text, with a quick task to find the main idea.
• An audio clip, played twice, with a short listening task.
• A model answer, such as a good email, with the features underlined.
• A short talk by you, with a few questions to check.
Tips:
• Give a task before students read or listen. This gives them a reason.
• Keep teacher talk short. Show, do not tell.
• Check meaning with simple questions, not 'Do you understand?'.
• Let students compare answers in pairs before whole class feedback.

ex.t: Check meaning in a better way
b: Poor: 'Do you understand?'
Better: 'Show me with your fingers: is the answer one, two or three?'
Better: 'Tell your partner what the writer wants.'

p: In guided practice students use the new language with support. The task is controlled. There is a clear right answer or model, so students can succeed.
Examples:
• Gap fill and matching exercises.
• Making sentences from prompts.
• Pair drills with a model dialogue.
• Rewriting a paragraph with better linking words.
Walk around and listen. Do not sit at your desk. Note common errors on a small piece of paper for feedback later. Help only when needed. Keep praise specific: 'Good, you used 'although' correctly.'
Aim for a mix of interaction patterns: students working alone for one to two minutes, then pairs, then groups of three or four, then whole class.

b: Individual: thinking time.
Pair: more talk for every student.
Group: ideas and roles.
Whole class: sharing and feedback.

p: In free production students use the language to do a real task. They choose their own words. This is the phase where fluency grows.
Examples:
• A short talk on a Part 2 style card.
• A group discussion with a Part 3 question.
• Writing an email or a report from a stimulus.
• A role play at a shop or a help desk.

Give clear instructions, then step back. Write the timing on the board. During the task, do not correct every mistake. Listen and collect. After the task give feedback on three to five key language points, good and bad.
This phase is where students get most speaking and writing time. If you must shorten the lesson, shorten the earlier phases, not this one.

b: Say them once, in short sentences.
Show an example.
Check with one question: 'What are you going to do first?'
Start the timer.

p: The plenary brings the lesson back to the objective. It is not a goodbye. It is the moment when you and your students see what was learned.
Good plenaries:
• Students say or write one new thing they can now do.
• A quick quiz of three questions.
• A 'traffic light' check: green (I can do it), amber (I need practice), red (I need help).
• Students read a sentence they wrote today.
Use what you learn. If most students show red or amber, change tomorrow's plan. Write a short note in your lesson record. A plenary you ignore wastes time.

b: Look back at the objective. Did most students reach it?
What will I change tomorrow?
Who needs extra help?

p: Copy this template. Fill it in for every lesson. After some weeks you will not need to write everything, but the thinking should stay.
• Class, date and lesson number.
• Topic and syllabus skill codes.
• Lesson objective and two success criteria.
• Prior knowledge: what do they already know?
• Materials: texts, audio, cards, board work, technology and backup.
• Stages table: time, stage, teacher activity, student activity, interaction pattern.
• Possible problems and my plan for them.
• Differentiation: support, core and stretch tasks.
• Assessment: how I will check learning.
• Homework.
• After the lesson: what went well, what to change.

b: 0 to 6: Starter. Teacher shows picture. Students write words. Individual then pair.
6 to 18: Input. Teacher reads model email. Students underline. Pairs.
18 to 30: Guided practice. Students match openings and endings. Pairs.
30 to 45: Free production. Students plan and write. Individual.
45 to 53: Plenary. Students check with a checklist. Pairs.
53 to 55: Close. Homework.

sections.h: A full sample lesson: an informal email about a problem
p: Here is a complete 55 minute lesson, written for this course. It practises Paper 1, Exercise 5. A task like this appears in the 2024 specimen paper, where students write an email to a friend about a problem with something they bought online.

Objective: Students can write an informal email that explains why they bought something, describes a problem and says what they will do. Skill codes W1, W2, W4. Success criteria: I covered all three bullet points. I used friendly language. I linked ideas with 'so', 'because' and 'but'.
Materials: model email on paper, task sheet, checklist, a timer.
Starter (0 to 6 minutes): Students write the names of three things they bought online or in a shop and one problem each. Pair share.

Input (6 to 16 minutes): Read a model email. Students underline friendly phrases (Guess what! You won't believe this) and linking words. Answer three questions: Why did the writer buy it? What is the problem? What will the writer do?
Guided practice (16 to 28 minutes): Students match sentence openings to endings; rewrite three formal sentences in a friendly way (I would like to inform you becomes Guess what!).

Free production (28 to 45 minutes): Read the task: You recently bought an item online. There was a problem with it. Write an email to a friend. Explain why you bought the item, describe the problem, say what you are going to do. Write about 120 to 160 words. Students plan three paragraphs in two minutes, then write for 12 minutes.
Plenary (45 to 53 minutes): Swap emails. Use a checklist: Did the writer cover three points? Is it friendly? Are there linking words? Give two stars and a wish.
Close (53 to 55 minutes): Homework: improve the email using your partner's wish.
Differentiation: support with sentence starters; core with the checklist; stretch with a challenge to use two less common phrases.

b: Students see a model before writing.
They practise the language in small steps first.
They write for a real reader.
They check their work with a clear tool.

activity: Write a 55 minute lesson plan for one skill from Paper 1 or Paper 3. Use the template. Include a starter, three main phases, a plenary and a differentiation note. Teach it, then write three lines about what you would change.

check.q: About how long should the free production phase last in a 55 minute lesson?
Which is the main purpose of a plenary?
o: To check learning against the lesson objective
To give out the homework only

check.q: If a lesson is running late, what should you shorten?
o: The earlier phases, not the free production or plenary
